titre: Under a Roman Fort, Letters Rather Than Annals
accroche: At Vindolanda, the mud preserved what Rome wrote day to day: a birthday invitation sits beside a request for socks
contenu_vulgarise:
Beneath the Roman fort of Vindolanda, near Hadrian's Wall, the ground has stayed saturated with water for two thousand years. This shell of compacted straw and fern, sealed by pockets of clay, deprived bacteria of the oxygen they need to destroy wood. The result: letters written in ink, on thin sheets of wood the size of a postcard, have come through the centuries without decomposing.

The archaeologist Robin Birley unearths the first fragments in March 1973, at the bottom of an excavation trench. Since then, more than 1,700 tablets have been brought to light at the site, most of them written between 85 and 130 CE, when the auxiliary garrison is already holding the frontier, even before the wall is built.

## What they tell

One might expect a military archive to hold food accounts and strength reports. And there are some: one tablet counts the soldiers present, absent, or sick. But the bulk of the corpus, since edited by the papyrologists Alan Bowman and David Thomas, is made up of private writings.

A soldier receives a package containing socks, two pairs of sandals, and two pairs of underpants; the sandals are mentioned twice in the letter, probably because two relatives each sent a pair. A military report calls the local Britons brittunculi, “wretched little Britons,” the first known occurrence of this contemptuous diminutive.

And then there is tablet 291. Around 100 CE, Claudia Severa writes to Sulpicia Lepidina, wife of the fort's commander, to invite her to her birthday. The letter is dictated to a scribe, but the closing line is added in another hand, less regular, more careful: that of Claudia Severa herself. It is the oldest known Latin text written in a woman's hand.

## The shift

The spontaneous image of a fort of the Roman Empire is that of a military machine: legions, discipline, conquest. Vindolanda shows something else, life going on behind the frontier, made of invitations, family mail, packages against the cold.

It is not that the military story is false; the strength reports are there in the same archives. It is that the overwhelming majority of what a garrison wrote day to day had nothing martial about it. And that majority would never have reached us had it not been trampled into airless mud, a few meters under a fort from which annals were expected, and which kept letters instead.

quiz.question: Why is Vindolanda tablet 291 an exceptional document?
choix: It gives the first complete organizational chart of a Roman garrison in Britain
It is the only Vindolanda tablet written entirely by a professional scribe
It is the oldest known Latin writing traced by a woman's own hand
It proves that Vindolanda was built before the rest of Hadrian's Wall
quiz.explication: The letter is dictated to a scribe, but Claudia Severa adds the closing line in her own hand: it is this passage, not any military content, that makes it the oldest known female Latin writing. The other options describe things the tablets do not show.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why did the wood of the Vindolanda tablets come through two thousand years without decomposing?
choix: Because it was coated with a protective resin before being buried
Because the Romans used a wood particularly resistant to rot
Because the waterlogged ground deprived bacteria of the oxygen needed for decomposition
Because the tablets were kept in a permanently heated building
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The water-saturated ground, sealed by pockets of clay, deprived bacteria of the oxygen they need to destroy wood, allowing it to be preserved.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who unearthed the first tablet fragments at Vindolanda, in March 1973?
choix: A team from the Paris Observatory
Claudia Severa herself, rediscovered by later excavations
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is the archaeologist Robin Birley who unearths the first fragments in March 1973, at the bottom of an excavation trench.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why is the word brittunculi, found on a military tablet, notable?
choix: It is the first known occurrence of this contemptuous diminutive for the local Britons
It is the first Latin word ever found on a medium other than stone
It is an affectionate term soldiers used among themselves
It is the name of a military unit stationed at Vindolanda
quiz_supplementaire.explication: A military report calls the local Britons brittunculi, wretched little Britons: the first known occurrence of this contemptuous diminutive.
